extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory/public affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Expository political-theory treatment of how the social principle of equality shapes popular opinions, sentiments, and institutional tendencies—especially toward centralized government and loss of intermediate powers. It identifies mechanisms and incidental causes that promote or inhibit centralization in democratic societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality gives men a taste for free institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of equality, which makes men independent of each other, gives them a habit and a taste for following, in their private actions, no other guide but their own will. This independence tends to make them look upon all authority with a jealous eye, and speedily suggests to them the notion and the love of political freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: equality produces individual independence and an instinctive love of political independence; this prepares citizens to value governments whose heads they elect and whose administration they can control. Anticipated consequence: a bias to free institutions is the first and most visible political effect of equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality generates two opposing tendencies (anarchy vs. servitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of equality begets two tendencies; the one leads men straight to independence, and may suddenly drive them into anarchy; the other conducts them by a longer, more secret, but more certain road, to servitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: democratic instincts produce both a visible risk of disorder and a subtler drift toward submission to central power—nations perceive the danger of anarchy and resist it, but the gradual move to servitude is less noticed and thus more dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic notions favor the concentration of power
rubrics_metrics.description: In democratic ages the notion of a sole and central power which governs the whole community by its direct influence arises naturally; the notion of secondary powers is wanting and complicated systems are repugnant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elaboration: democratic intellects prefer simple, general notions and conceive government as a single central authority; this predisposes societies to centralize administrative and legislative authority rather than preserve intermediate bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for uniformity of legislation in democratic societies
rubrics_metrics.description: The very next notion to that of a sole and central power is the notion of uniformity of legislation: as every man sees that he differs but little from those about him, he cannot understand why a rule which is applicable to one man should not be equally applicable to all others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: small privileges or legal distinctions become odious; uniform rules are seen as a first condition of good government in democratic thought, weakening support for localized or particularized legal arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments of democratic nations predispose them to support central power
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits and sentiments—such as lack of habitual superiors/inferiors, busy private life, love of tranquillity, and dependence combined with independence—lead citizens to abandon public business to the State and to look to the central power for support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: private preoccupation and the desire for public tranquillity cause individuals to surrender rights or seek help from the State; over time the permanence and stability of central power absorbs more functions because citizens neither have time nor inclination to govern locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hatred of privilege fuels centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: The hatred which men bear to privilege increases as privileges become more scarce and less considerable; this hatred sets democratic peoples against the smallest privileges and favors concentrating political rights in the hands of the State's representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: citizens prefer stripping 'neighbors' of prerogatives while conceding broad powers to the impersonal sovereign; central power is less envied and more readily empowered because it stands above individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual sympathy between central government and citizens in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity and common tastes create a secret and lasting sympathy between the sovereign and every member of the community; public confidence is only reluctantly withdrawn and is often restored quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result: even when citizens dislike the persons who govern, they often love the power itself; faults of government are frequently forgiven because its aims and tastes align with popular sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical legacy (prior experience of freedom) moderates centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Among people who have lived free long before they became equal, tendencies derived from free institutions combat those derived from equality; private members of such communities will never entirely forfeit their independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Americans retained trial by jury, free speech, local autonomy—because equality there is of more recent date and freedom older, they resisted full centralization. Thus historical institutional inheritance can prevent or slow centralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of achieving equality (revolutionary vs. gradual) affects centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: When equality is obtained suddenly by violent revolution, local class leaders are swept away and the State alone seems capable of administering affairs, making centralization more inevitable; where equality grew without revolution, centralization is less rapid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: abrupt social upheaval that destroys intermediate powers tends to channel their functions into the central state; conversely, continuity of local institutions protects decentralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and intelligence condition the ability to sustain secondary powers
rubrics_metrics.description: In ages of equality men require much intelligence, knowledge, and art to organize and maintain secondary powers; concentration of power increases in proportion as democratic societies are ignorant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: central power can draw the limited cultivation available in the country to its advantage, creating an intellectual gap between rulers and citizens that facilitates governance from the centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: War and military requirements accelerate centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralization is useful for war because success depends on transferring all the resources of a nation to a single point; men of military genius are fond of centralization and increase the powers of the central government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: nations exposed to frequent or great wars tend more rapidly toward expanded state functions and centralized administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and sympathies of the ruler influence centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: The attraction of administrative powers to the centre is less rapid under kings connected with the old aristocratic order than under new princes who are children of democratic achievements; rulers who 'love equality' more readily centralize power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: rulers whose background aligns with equality and who appear to represent it will gain broad confidence and thus can centralize with less resistance; aristocratic origins can slow centralization because of shared prejudices with local elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporary European trend toward increasing governmental power
rubrics_metrics.description: Among European nations the State has resumed attributes of sovereign power formerly held by private persons and corporations; local authorities and privileges are disappearing and secondary powers are being concentrated in the hands of the sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: many charitable and social functions once managed privately are now administered by the State; this is presented as a pervasive historical tendency rather than a normative prescription.
